title: Federal Judge Rules DHS Likely Violated Rochester Man's First Amendment Rights Over Anti-ICE Email
detail: U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras (D.D.C.) ruled on Tuesday, September 15, 2026 that David Streever, a Rochester, New York resident, is likely to succeed on his claim that DHS and ICE violated his First Amendment rights after he emailed then-Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons in January criticizing the immigration crackdown in Minnesota. Two ICE agents delivered a 'Warning Notice' to Streever's home on June 23, 2026 and separately tried to contact him at a hotel, warning him that continuing his conduct could lead to prosecution. In a 43-page opinion, Contreras wrote that 'Mr. Streever has a right to express his political views through non-threatening speech, however degrading the speech might be,' and that the Warning Notice 'practically shouts' that Streever could be prosecuted if he keeps speaking out. The preliminary injunction bars DHS and ICE from relying on the notice, from using the January email as grounds for prosecution or investigative demands while the case proceeds, and from issuing similar warnings suggesting that non-threatening criticism of the government is unlawful.

title: Washington Post Investigation: ICE Quietly Firing New Hires Over Vetting Gaps After Recruit's Suicide
detail: The Washington Post reported September 15, 2026 that ICE has been quietly dismissing officers hired during last year's rapid recruitment surge — which offered $50,000 signing bonuses and expedited training to bring on roughly 12,000 new deportation officers and investigative agents after the 'One Big Beautiful Bill' funding — after discovering background problems that former DHS officials say should have blocked their hiring in the first place. An ICE whistleblower warned the Office of Inspector General in August 2025 that applicants 'were being cleared for duty without fingerprints, identity verification or credit checks.' The story centers on Joseph Moore, a 38-year-old Marine reservist and father of two who had been rejected by multiple law enforcement agencies before ICE hired him as a deportation officer in autumn 2025; he died by suicide outside ICE's Philadelphia field office on August 28, 2026, one day after receiving his termination notice — which arrived one day before his one-year anniversary and three days after he filed a workers' compensation claim. The city medical examiner ruled the death a suicide from a self-inflicted gunshot wound; Moore's family disputes that finding. ICE informed all deportation officers of Moore's death by email after Post inquiries and said the incident is under investigation.
